rationale: The hypothesis posits that dysmorphic facial features in GTF3C3-related neurodevelopmental disorder (OMIM #621201) are distinctly recognizable in infancy and early childhood but evolve or attenuate with age, hindering clinical identification in adolescents and adults. While Abdel-Hamid et al. described distinctive facial dysmorphisms that appeared recognizable in very young children (n=4), the larger multicenter study by De Hayr et al. (n=12) characterized the craniofacial findings as 'variable nonfamilial facial features', suggesting lack of a uniform recognizable gestalt regardless of age. Furthermore, López et al. described an adult patient (aged 27) with persistent 'mild facial dysmorphic features', indicating that facial anomalies do not completely disappear with age. True longitudinal progression/attenuation has not been formally demonstrated across cohorts.

evidence.text: Abdel et al. identified biallelic GTF3C3 variants in 4 patients from 3 unrelated families, noting microcephaly, developmental delay, intellectual disability, and distinctive dysmorphic facies that appeared recognizable in very young children.

source.title: Biallelic variants in GTF3C3 encoding a subunit of the TFIIIC2 complex are associated with neurodevelopmental phenotypes in humans and zebrafish
source.quote: The patients exhibited microcephaly, developmental delay, intellectual disability and distinctive dysmorphic facies that appear recognizable in very young children.

evidence.text: De Hayr et al. evaluated 12 affected individuals from 7 families and characterized the facial presentation as variable nonfamilial facial features rather than a cohesive, recognizable syndrome-specific facial gestalt.

source.title: Biallelic variants in GTF3C3 result in an autosomal recessive disorder with intellectual disability
source.quote: The cohort presented with intellectual disability, variable nonfamilial facial features, motor impairments, seizures, and cerebellar/corpus callosum malformations.

evidence.text: López et al. reported the oldest described individual with GTF3C3 variants (controlled seizures at age 27), presenting with mild dysmorphic facial features alongside global developmental delay, intellectual disability, and structural neurological findings.

source.quote: She had mild facial dysmorphic features including long... oldest reported individual so far... controlled at age 27

conflicts: Abdel-Hamid et al. (2025) reported that facial features form a 'distinctive dysmorphic facies that appear recognizable in very young children', whereas De Hayr et al. (2025) analyzed 12 patients across 7 families and identified only 'variable nonfamilial facial features', contradicting the premise of a shared, recognizable childhood facial gestalt.

Longitudinal attenuation of dysmorphisms in adolescents and adults remains unproven: while adult patients have mild facial findings, systematic serial craniofacial photographic analysis across developmental stages has not been performed to separate attenuation from baseline phenotypic variability.

new_directions.question_text: Does 3D facial photogrammetry across age cohorts demonstrate statistically significant age-dependent loss of dysmorphic vectors in GTF3C3 patients?
new_directions.rationale: Objective computational phenotyping (e.g., GestaltMatcher or Face2Gene) comparing infant/toddler versus adolescent/adult facial scans would quantify whether dysmorphic features attenuate or simply display baseline inter-familial heterogeneity.

new_directions.question_text: Do non-craniofacial neurological features (e.g., cerebellar atrophy, simplified gyral pattern, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum) provide superior diagnostic discrimination over facial dysmorphism across all age groups?
new_directions.rationale: Because facial dysmorphism is variable or mild, neuroimaging phenotypes reported across Abdel, De Hayr, and López may serve as more robust discriminant criteria for OMIM #621201.
